title: Fukanzazengi Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk explores the concept of reality and understanding, drawing on the teachings of Dogen, a Japanese priest who wrote "Fukanzazengi", a text on Zen practice that challenges traditional notions of enlightenment as something to be achieved through meditation or effort. Instead, Dogen's text suggests that reality is already perfect and all-pervading, and that true understanding comes from recognizing what is already present, rather than trying to fix or change it. This approach encourages a sense of immediacy and non-separation, inviting readers to explore the depths of their own experience without attachment to concepts like separation and lack.

sentences.text: Thanks for being here.
Just to try to explain a little confusing form: on Wednesday night, we always start with meditation, and then there's a kind of rotating schedule of events after the meditation.
On this schedule, two of the Wednesdays have talks, one of which is a formal dharma talk, longer, more ritualized, quieter.
The person giving the talk has to have gone through the empowerment of having been the head student at a practice period, the empowerment for giving a formal dharma talk.
So that's usually the second Wednesday of the month.
And then on the fourth Wednesday of the month, we have a time on the schedule for a student talk, so a little less formal, informal.
It doesn't have to be somebody who has been head student at a practice period.
It certainly doesn't have to be me.
But if nobody signed up, then I do it.
So that's my karma.
I did ask John to do the next one.
Of course, John can do either, so it's still confusing, but any of us can do this student talk.
And it doesn't have to be a prepared talk.
I prepared a little thing, but you could just bring in a book you've been studying or an article in a magazine, or you can even just bring in an experience you've had.
I remember one time we had a whole student talk about how somebody yelled at me on the road, and we sort of talked about that and processed: what is that, to be yelled at on the road?
We all have that experience.
How do you practice with that?
So you don't have to have anything too brilliant to say.
If you would like to give the student talk in June, that would be great.
You could even bring a book that you thought was interesting and meant to read, and then we can pass it around.
So in other words, something connected to Buddhism is good probably, but there's no sort of committee that evaluates your presentation.

It's just a way, and it's really valuable actually for the person who is in the hot seat too, because just trying to express something, trying to say something about Dharma and about practice, really helps to clarify what you are doing, what this is.
Now, we heard the rain earlier.
It was beautiful.
I was remembering a story that Gary Snyder tells, secondhand; I haven't heard Gary Snyder say this, but I heard somebody say he said it.

When he was practicing Zen in Kyoto in the fifties, at a little temple there, and I was in Kyoto last summer, so I have more of a sense of this, he said that during the summer practice period it would rain a lot.
When it rains there in the raining season, he's been there too, it rains really hard, the kind of thing where you duck into shelter and wait about 15 minutes because it's not safe to drive or walk.
It rains really hard.
And Gary Snyder apparently was saying that for whatever reason, it would always be raining really hard when the teacher gave the talk.
The teacher was a very soft spoken person, and he was also speaking in Japanese, which Gary I think was reasonably fluent in, but there's fluent and there's fluent.
I've been studying Spanish, and I was at the gym, and a couple of guys were speaking Spanish in the shower room, where the acoustics are such, you know what I mean?
I couldn't make out a word.
I was like, wow, there's knowing a little Spanish and there's knowing a little Spanish.
So Gary knows some Japanese, but he said he basically couldn't understand a word of any of these talks for this long training period.
Somehow it was okay.
He just did the schedule and appreciated being there and worked with the things that you work with, doing Zen training, and listened to the rain.
But then he said, many years later, it started coming to him.
He started realizing what the teacher had been saying in those talks, I don't know how much, 20 or 30 years later, something like that.
I thought of that story when it was raining, because there are different kinds of knowing, you know what I mean?
Different ways of knowing.
And maybe we're a little bit oriented around one particular kind of knowing.
That kind of story points out that there are other kinds of knowing, other kinds of listening, and things that are always working at a lot of different levels.
Speaking of work on different levels, I thought I would say a little more about Dogen.
A couple of weeks ago, we talked about an essay by Dogen.
Tonight, I thought we'd look a little bit at the first part of another Dogen essay, which is in our chant book, and we chant it sometimes.
I thought, wouldn't that be nice, to just spend a little more time reading that together and thinking about it?
Maybe I could say a few things to pique your interest.
This is the text in the chant book called Fukanzazengi, page 13, page 13.
Dogen was a Japanese priest who is credited with bringing this way of practice to Japan, which then came to America in the 1950s or so.
And now here we are.

He wrote this text, Fukanzazengi, which I've translated, I put a name on there, as Dogen's Universal Recommendation for Zazen, which is pretty close, close enough, I guess, to what those characters mean.
He wrote it in 1227, when he was only 27 years old.
It's really handy, he was born in the year 1200, so it's easy to calculate his age.
Of course, he wouldn't have called it that, but we call it that.
It was pretty soon after he returned from his sort of epic voyage to China, his travels to China, where he was for three or four years studying Zen.
He wrote it after he had established a small monastery on the outskirts of Kyoto, south of Kyoto, so not far from where Gary Snyder was in the 1950s, or where Dogen was in 1227.

And just a few textual notes in case you're interested: most of the essays he wrote that were collected in the Shobogenzo collection, his famous collection of essays, were written in Japanese, which was unusual.
The high culture of the time was all written down in Chinese, using just Chinese characters.
Poetry, religion and literature were written using just the Chinese characters.
Maybe it's a little bit like church Latin, if you're fluent in Italian, maybe that's sort of parallel, but a little different, because what the Japanese did is their own spoken language evolved.
And then at some point, I don't know when, they borrowed the entire Chinese character set, sort of wholesale, and used it for their own purposes.
So most of the characters mean basically the same thing in Japan as in China, but they're pronounced in a different way.
And actually many of the meanings and some of the forms are changed.
Then the Japanese, to suit the way that they speak, had to add additional ideographic characters like that.
They also created a whole phonetic syllabary to stitch the grammar together.
So it's a very strange language, really weird.
Anyway, it's interesting he wrote this in Chinese, because a lot of the text later on he wrote in Japanese, so maybe he just wasn't comfortable yet writing in Japanese.
What's interesting about this text is that it's a very forceful text on Zazen practice, very clear and emphatic.
In a way it was expressing his plan.
It's like his mission statement, Dogen's mission statement for the rest of his life.
And he basically stuck to this mission for the rest of his life with a great amount of energy and productivity.
He wrote a tremendous number of texts and started an important monastery, but it wasn't really until later that all this snowballed.
He probably only had some couple hundred students, maybe, not thousands and thousands, not great audiences.
So anyway, it starts out, and you can read along or you can just listen, it doesn't matter.
It starts out with a really strange beginning, because it's a recommendation for doing meditation practice, right?
I was thinking, how would we sell meditation practice if we were going to write a text for Time magazine or something like that?
We would probably sell it by first, as you would, expressing the problem.
Maybe we'd give a little example: Sally was on her way to work and feeling tense.
Then you'd probably talk about the problem in some systematic scientific way: people in America suffer from increasing incidences of this and that, stress and so on.
And then you'd have experts, right?
I mean, we know the structure.
But this is a very different structure, because it starts with the opposite.
It starts by saying things are perfect.
Actually, things are perfect.
*The way is basically perfect and all pervading.
And how could it be contingent upon practice and realization?*
So it starts out by saying that whatever this thing is that you think you're going to get from practice, it's already here.
It's all pervading.
It's everywhere.
It's beyond something that you could create by doing something.
It says it right away.
So it seems like a backwards recommendation for Zazen.
He's basically saying this is not going to work, because there's nothing that needs to be done.
I found a wonderful resource online.
If you ask me, I can send you a link to it.
They go through this whole text character by character, and they actually have photographs of a copy of Dogen's text, not the 1227 version but the 1232 text.
So they have the actual characters, probably by Dogen, and what they mean.
And it doesn't actually say perfect.
So maybe perfect isn't the best word.
Perfect might be a triggering word for us.
One of the characters in this first section is the character for a circle, or going around.
So another translation might be that the way, or the real way, circulates everywhere.
It's in circulation, with all the levels of meaning that implies.
The blood circulates, we circulate, the air circulates, right?
There's the water cycle, the carbon cycle, so the way maybe has that quality.
It's not fixed.
It's like some sort of natural cycle of some kind.
So that might be better than perfect, but we got the translation that we got, so that's okay.
I'm not even sure where our translation came from.
We inherited it from San Francisco Zen Center.
Anyway, this opening expresses what was Dogen's big question in his life and his practice.
Essentially, the teachings of Buddhism, and maybe some inner feeling he was having even as a boy, both say things are just the way they need to be.
We have Buddha, we have some awakening nature, Buddha nature, and there's a sense of how could things be any other than this?
This is just what it is, right?
So we would say perfect, but not perfect like perfection.
That being the case, why are there all these problems?
Why do we need to practice?
Why are we so upset and confused?
It doesn't make sense, it doesn't add up.

That was supposedly his question, and a lot of our supposition about Dogen's biography, and what made him tick, is really just reading between the lines of his writing and some biographies of him that were written later, after his death.
So who knows really what happened, but that's the sense you get from Dogen: that he was driven by some question.
Things are okay, and they're not okay.
The way is perfect and all pervading, and yet there's some need to practice, some need to realize something.
So then it says:
*The Dharma vehicle is free and untrammeled.
What need is there for concentrated effort?*
And another translation I saw: "The essential teaching is fully available.
How could effort be necessary?"
Another way to look at that: the essential teaching is fully available.
How could effort be necessary?
So, the same point.
And indeed, "the whole body is far beyond the world's dust.
Who could believe in a means to wash it clean or to brush it clean?"
Now, whenever you're talking about dust and brushing dust off things, it's usually a reference to a very famous Zen story.
So I've got to tell you the Zen story.
That's the other thing that's interesting about Dogen, which you can [unclear: "drag your nuts"] actually: every paragraph is packed with references, and I knew only some of them.
There's more and more material available, and you can find translations online, in other places, that have credible numbers of footnotes.
Not this one so much, but another one I looked at: the first paragraph had like four pages of notes.
The first half of this sentence is a reference to this story, and the second half of that sentence is a reference to that story.
The stories sort of connect, and I sort of know them.
Anyway, this reference here about brushing dust clean is about the very famous story of the sixth ancestor.
These are kind of family stories of our school, so I've got to tell them to you.
Are they important?
Are they true?
It's hard to know.
It's hard to know.
This story is about a man in China in, I guess, the fifth century, named Huineng.
They constructed a lineage later.
They constructed a lineage because the sense of ancestors is very important all through Asia, and you can kind of feel that when you're in Asia.
So this is a story about Huineng, who was later credited as the sixth Zen ancestor in China, Bodhidharma being the first.
He was number six.
Huineng was a very impoverished person, born into a poor family.
His parents died when he was young, and he made his living delivering firewood.
I don't know if he was a teenager or something like that.
One time he was delivering firewood to a small temple, and he heard a priest in the temple reciting a Buddhist sutra called the Diamond Sutra.
A phrase in there (some versions tell you which phrase, I forget which one) really struck him very deeply.
He had a really big aha moment, like an awakening, enlightenment kind of moment.
That sounds very grand and dramatic, and Zen stories are full of these.
But I think we know experientially what that is, too.
Right?
That's a feeling that we get sometimes, and maybe this is a big one of those.
So he knows that he has to find out about this, about the Buddhism, about the sutra.
He asked for recommendations and he ends up at the monastery of a well-known teacher in those days named Hongren, who was the fifth ancestor later.
It's a kind of class system, sadly, right?
The monks are educated, smart people to some extent, somewhat refined in some way.
So the teacher recognized that this illiterate guy probably wouldn't fit in very well in the monastery, and he sent him to the kitchen.
Huineng is in there chopping wood and stoking the fires.
It's a big monastery, with these huge woks, I've seen pictures, like this big, so you've got to keep the fire going.
That was his job.
The story goes that one day Hongren, who was getting close to retirement, made an announcement.
This is the announcement as it was recorded a couple hundred years later, but I'm sure that's what he said.
It's great, religious history in general is great this way.
Especially so, they map all kinds of wonderful things onto the previous generations.
So here's what he said.
*The question of incessant rebirth is a momentous one.
The question of incessant rebirth is a momentous one.
Day after day, instead of trying to free yourself from the bitter sea of life and death, you seem to go after tainted merits, only tainted actions.
Yet these actions will be of no help.
If your essence of mind is obscured, go and seek for wisdom in your own mind and write me a poem about it.
He who understands the essence of mind will be given the robe and the Dharma.*
So in other words, you'll be the new abbot.
You get the job, you get the robe and the Dharma, the robe and the bowl.
*And I shall make him the sixth patriarch.
Go away quickly. [unclear: "I get to work."]*
So this is, in a way, another version of Dogen's question, right?
This question of suffering: how can we ignore this question of suffering and just watch TV and do whatever it is we do?
How could that be?
He's saying, how could it be that you follow any action that's not just to get to the bottom of this?
So look into that deeply and write me a poem expressing how you're going to do that.
How are you going to free yourself from this?
*Delay not in writing.* Blah, blah, blah.
It just repeats the whole thing over again.
Anyway, everyone figured, though, so there was a presumptive error, like there is in every organization, right?
The presumptive error was the head monk, the shoo-in.
At the time, although it seems like it's more than just for a training period, maybe it's a head monk for a long time, a guy named Shenxiu, and he was kind of a shoo-in for the job.
Everyone figured he would write the poem and be the abbot.
There was sort of no point in anyone else trying.
It's embarrassing, you know, you don't embarrass yourself, right?
So-and-so is going to get the promotion, so you don't put yourself forward.
But the story goes that Shenxiu was a little bit insecure about his understanding, and he didn't really want to write the poem.
He just wanted things to go smoothly forward, with seniority carrying him into the [unclear: "avid ship"].
So he decided to write his poem anonymously and wait and see if Hongren approved, and then he'd take credit for it or not.
The story goes he wrote this on the wall.
I don't know if they usually wrote things on the walls, but it was a very strange thing to write on the walls.
I don't know.
So the head monk, Shenzhui, wrote this on the wall:
*The body is a Bodhi tree.
The mind a standing mirror bright.
At all times polish it diligently and let no dust alight.*
Bodhi is like the tree the Buddha was enlightened under, right, the Bodhi tree.
So: the body is a Bodhi tree.
The mind is a standing mirror bright.
Apparently it literally means "mirror stand," but that doesn't make any sense in English, so it gets changed to "a standing mirror bright."
At all times polish it diligently and let no dust alight.
So this is the practice side of this question, right?
This is real.
This is a really good poem, right?
Practice with the body.
The body is where awakening happens.
It's not some idea; the body is where you sit.
The mind is a mirror.
So don't think that the mind has its own existence and knows something.
The mind is just reflecting all the phenomena that happen in some way.
So there's a recognition of that process, and that the mind is in some ways defiled and messed up and confused by greed and delusion and attachment.
And we need to clean things up.
We need to polish the mind so we don't suffer as much and create so much suffering.
And we should be so thorough that no dust can alight there.
So: practical, continuous practice.
Later, Dogen wrote an essay called "Continuous Practice."
So it sounds pretty good.
And I think when I first heard this story, I misunderstood, thinking this was the stupid poem, and later the good poem's coming.
You can see the other foot, right?
But this is a good poem.
This is a good understanding.
And Hongren apparently said publicly that this was a really good poem, and told the sangha, "Oh, very good.
Practice according to this poem.
You will not fall into the evil realms and you will receive great benefit.
Light incense and pay respect to this poem.
Recite it and you'll see your essential nature."
So he's a very supportive teacher.

And the other thing about this story that's nice, which I never thought of before, is that a lot of the stories about the [unclear: "answers"] sound like really tough guys, and they're always whacking people.
And this is a very supportive teacher.
And as you'll see, he didn't completely agree with this poem, but he was very supportive of his student.
And [unclear: "my our sort of guide to Jerome and Fisher"] is that way: very supportive, always supportive.
So all the [unclear: "typos"] did so wonderful.
But privately, apparently, the teacher told the [unclear: "gentui"] that it wasn't really that great.
He told him privately:
*You've arrived at the gate, but you haven't entered with this level of understanding.
You have no idea what the supreme body mind is.
Upon hearing my words, you should immediately recognize the original mind, the essential nature, which is unborn and unceasing at all times.
See it clearly in every thought.
And the mind with the mind free from hindrances.
In the one reality, everything is real.
Phenomena are just as they are.*
So that's kind of, "Good.
Please go deeper.
Please go deeper."
Meanwhile, we have our woodcutter in the kitchen.
Remember Huineng?
And he is illiterate, right?
So he couldn't read the poem, but they all were reciting it and talking about it.
So in the kitchen, they were talking about it.
He heard it, and he thought to himself, huh, that's interesting.
That's not quite how I see it.
So he asked one of the temple administrators to write out a poem on the wall for him, also anonymously.
And his poem is this:
*Bodhi is fundamentally without any tree.
The bright mirror is not a stand, or doesn't have a stand.
Fundamentally, there is not a single thing.
Where could any dust be attracted?*
So he's bringing up the emptiness side of this.
Oh, so you think there's dust?
Where'd you get this idea?
Why are you clinging to these ideas, defilement and needing to fix it?
Once you think it's wrong, it's a very limited view.
Please release from that.
This is kind of his attitude.
I'm not going to read it at this point.
I'm not going to read the poem. [unclear: "I'm going to read the poem.
I'm going to read the poem.
That's the main idea.
And then he said, oh, I don't know if I should read it."] That's the main idea.
And I'll try to not tell you the rest of this, because it goes on and on.
So basically the teacher knew right away who had written the poem, and gave the robe and the bowl to Huineng, but knew it would be a big problem in the monastery.
So Huineng snuck out, and there's this whole complicated drama, a wonderful supernatural drama where all the monks chase after him.
There's a chase scene.
And we'll have to tell you this one part.
At one point, Huineng sees that they're coming after him and says, okay, I'll put the bowl down, because you see the symbols of office, right, this set of eating bowls and a special robe.
He says, okay, I'll put the bowl down on this rock, and you may have it if you can take it.
And of course, just like the sword in the stone or something, he can't lift it.
Anyway, it's great stuff.
So, back to Dogen.
That's what's interesting about Zen writing: this whole long story is behind the sentence.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** *The whole body is far beyond the world's dust.
The whole body is far beyond the world's dust.* Where is there dust?
Why do you think your idea of the body is what the body is?
*And who could believe in a means to brush it clean?* So you see the reference there.
And then it goes on: *It is never apart from one, right where one is.
What is the use of going off here and there to practice?* There's a sense of the immediacy and non-separation of Dharma.
It's not apart from you, which is not the same as saying it is you.
It's not saying it's not you.
It's not apart from you.
It's right here.
That's the opening section of the text, bringing up this question of what Dharma is.
What is the nature of our living?
How could it be that we need to practice with this?
And yet we do.
Next time I'll keep working my way through this.
I'm going to take many talks, maybe.
It's funny, isn't it, these heavily loaded texts?
But it's really worth thinking about.
In the mindfulness classes they always say you really need to recognize how much there is right with you.
How much there is right with you.
There could be 99.9999% right with you, and then you'd focus on that little thing, right?
So *the way is perfect and all-pervading.* It's not apart from you, right where you are.
How could it be contingent upon you trying to fix it, you trying to do something?
So what is it about this sense of lack and separation, this need to do something?
And yet he goes on in the rest of the text to give very detailed instructions about what you should do.
It could just end there, right?
Okay, thank you, beautiful.
But then where does that leave us?
Kind of back where we started.
So it seems there's some experiential process of realizing that we're already home, that we're already complete.
As wise as the first poem was, it's rigidifying a certain sort of separation, a certain kind of lack.
So what do you think about the first three lines of this?
Yes, Elizabeth?
**Participant:** Well, because there's nowhere for the dust to land if the mirror is upright.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Oh, that's nice, yeah.
I'm going to use that analogy a lot in Dharma, being upright.
Yeah, being very upright.
Not leaning into your problems, not running from your problems.
Just being present.
That's nice.
There's more to get a handle on a little later in the text.

The other thing that's great about studying a text that we chant, and you can chant this if you start coming on Saturday mornings, is that we're having practice every Saturday morning, and as part of every other service we chant this text.
What's cool is that you internalize these things in a certain way, chanting them over and over and over again.
It kind of messes you up when they change the translation, but it happens.
This one they didn't change.
Sometimes phrases from these things just pop out when you need them.
There's a certain way that, through the text and through our practice of chanting, Dogen can teach us from the depths of history, or maybe he's never apart from us right where we are.
I don't know.
After chanting something for years and years and years, all of a sudden one word, half a sentence, explodes and takes on a whole new meaning.
Sometimes it's just a word or a sentence, or it seems that if I hang with any phrase, it does that.
**Participant:** Which makes me think that I think or speak.
That was a meditative process, like the pre-sentence.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
Yeah, that's a beautiful point.
It's like everything's deeper.
Right.
Yeah, and then we have a surface-level approach to meaning, in a way.
And any meaning will change.
Yeah, and ultimately it's just dissolving, and there's like, is there any meaning?
Like those avant-garde art pieces where you just repeat the same word over and over and over again.
What does it mean?
If you stare long enough, even at a common English word, you don't even know what you're looking at.
Like, what is this?
Yeah.
You've got to settle into it, yeah.
I wanted to try to remember, remember it.
Especially if you care about it.
Doing these things over and over again, just don't notice.
Yeah, maybe in a way that's culturally typical, this need for novelty and change.

If the effect of doing something with a tremendous amount of heart and repetition and simplicity and trust, like that trusting, somehow accesses a deeper meaning, it makes you wonder if the opposite is also true: if this emphasis on change and novelty and the new thing holds us in a surface level of meaning, forever.
You know what I mean?
A lot of people would agree with that.
Yeah, yeah.
Eye level, you know.
**Participant:** These things be, I was thinking about this and that, it just has to stay in.
And that's when you should...
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** You know, that seems really true, but then also what Jeff was saying seems equally so, that you don't have to worry.
You just trust, regardless of conditions.
And I think maybe they were saying that too, regardless of whether you're feeling really smart today or you're tired or you're alert or not, just listen, right?
Yeah, yeah.

If you've been coming and sitting with us on Wednesday evenings or something, and you haven't yet been to a day-long or a half-day-long or a three-day-long, you might consider giving it a try and seeing what's different.
And we have some coming up, as it happens.
Well, maybe it's time to stop.
Bob, you were about to say something.
Maybe it's gone.
**Participant:** It might have been.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Okay.
It'll come back to us.
